etymology: Greek angelos, messenger, and logia, discourse. Webster (1828) enters it as ANGELOL’OGY: “a discourse on angels; or the doctrine of angelic beings.”
biblical_def: Angelology is the part of doctrine that gathers what Scripture says about angels and goes no further. The Bible does not leave the subject vague. Angels are created spirits: God “maketh his angels spirits; his ministers a flaming fire” (Psa 104:4). They serve Him: “Bless the LORD, ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word” (Psa 103:20). They are sent to the saints: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?” (Heb 1:14). Christ Himself said of His little ones that “in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 18:10). Some fell: God “spared not the angels that sinned” (2Pe 2:4), and those “which kept not their first estate” are kept in chains “unto the judgment of the great day” (Jud 1:6). Their number is beyond counting: “ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands of thousands” (Rev 5:11). A sound angelology is therefore modest. It confesses what is written, worships the Lord of the angels and not the angels, and refuses to fill the silences of Scripture with invented names, ranks and messages.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ANGELOLOGY, a discourse on angels; the doctrine of angelic beings.
webster_full: A discourse on angels; or the doctrine of angelic beings.
scriptures: Who maketh his angels spirits; his ministers a flaming fire:
Bless the LORD, ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word.
Heb 1:14
Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?
For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment;
Col 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
corruption_summary: Popular religion turns angels into private guides and objects of devotion, the very thing Paul forbids as “worshipping of angels” (Col 2:18).
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is curiosity. Shelves of books name angels Scripture never names, sort them into ranks Scripture never gives, and report conversations Scripture never records. Paul calls this “intruding into those things which he hath not seen” (Col 2:18). What God has not revealed is not a gap for the imagination to fill.

The second corruption is devotion. Prayers to angels, guardian-angel cults and the hunt for angelic messages all move the eye from the Lord of hosts to His servants. The angels themselves refuse it. They do His commandments and hearken to His word (Psa 103:20); they are ministers, not mediators. The one Mediator between God and men is the man Christ Jesus, and a doctrine of angels that crowds Him is no longer Christian doctrine.

etymology: Greek anthropos, man, and morphe, form. Webster (1828) enters ANTHROPOMORPH’ISM as “the heresy of the anthropomorphites,” those who held that God has a bodily, human shape.
biblical_def: Anthropomorphism names the error of thinking that God has the form of a man. Webster (1828) calls it plainly “the heresy of the anthropomorphites.” Scripture shuts the door on it. “God is a Spirit” (Joh 4:24). At Horeb Israel “saw no manner of similitude” (Deu 4:15), and for that reason they were forbidden to make one. “God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent” (Num 23:19). Yet the same Bible speaks of the LORD’s hand and ear (Isa 59:1) and says “it repented the LORD that he had made man” (Gen 6:6). The two are not at war. God speaks of Himself in the language of men because men are the ones He is speaking to. His arm means His power, His eye His knowledge, His repenting a change in His dealings, not a change in Him: “I am the LORD, I change not” (Mal 3:6). The Westminster Confession states the doctrine in a line: God is “a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions” (WCF 2.1). Read human language of God as a figure, and Scripture is clear. Read it as a portrait, and you have made God “altogether such an one as thyself” (Psa 50:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ANTHROPOMORPHISM, the heresy of the anthropomorphites.
scriptures: Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Deu 4:15
Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
Gen 6:6
And it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.
Mal 3:6
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
These things hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself: but I will reprove thee, and set them in order before thine eyes.
corruption_summary: The old heresy gave God a body; its modern form gives Him changeable passions, a God who learns, waits and is surprised, built in the image of man.
corruption_paragraphs: The ancient anthropomorphites read the hand and arm of the LORD as limbs, and so pictured God in the shape of a man. The church answered from Joh 4:24 and Deu 4:15: God is a Spirit, and Israel saw no similitude. That answer still stands against every cult that teaches God has a body.

The modern form is subtler. It leaves God without a body but reads every figure of grief, repentance and surprise as a literal change in His being, until God is a fellow-sufferer who learns as history unfolds. That is anthropomorphism moved from the body to the soul. Scripture that says “it repented the LORD” (Gen 6:6) also says He “will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent” (1Sa 15:29). The figure must be read by the plain statement, never the plain statement by the figure.

pos: n. phrase (want of will, not want of faculty)
etymology: English moral, from Latin moralis (from mos, moris, manner), and inability, from Latin inhabilis. Webster (1828) has no separate headword; the phrase is his own, under INABIL’ITY, sense 3.
biblical_def: Moral inability is the bondage of a will that will not turn to God. Webster (1828) defines it exactly: “Want of moral power. Moral inability is considered to be want of inclination, disposition or will, or a deep-rooted aversion to act, and therefore improperly so called. Moral inability aggravates our guilt.” The phrase distinguishes two kinds of cannot. A lame man cannot walk; that is want of power in the body. A sinner cannot come to Christ; that is want of will in the heart, and it is no excuse. Christ put both sides in one sentence to the Jews: “ye will not come to me, that ye might have life” (Joh 5:40), and “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44). Paul says the carnal mind “is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7), and the natural man “receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God” (1Co 2:14). The sinner keeps every faculty, mind, heart and will; what he lacks is any love for God. That is why the inability condemns rather than excuses: he cannot because he will not. The Westminster Confession states it: man by the fall “hath wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation” (WCF 9.3). Only God, who quickens the dead (Eph 2:1), can give the will He commands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), INABILITY sense 3: want of moral power; want of inclination, disposition or will; a deep-rooted aversion to act. Moral inability aggravates our guilt.
webster_full: INABIL'ITY, noun [Latin inhabilis; in and habilis.]

3. Want of moral power. Moral inability is considered to be want of inclination, disposition or will, or a deep-rooted aversion to act, and therefore improperly so called. Moral inability aggravates our guilt.
MOR'AL, adjective [Latin moralis, from mos, moris, manner.]
2. Subject to the moral law and capable of moral actions; bound to perform social duties; as a moral agent or being.

Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
corruption_summary: One error says inability excuses the sinner, so God cannot command what man cannot do; the other says the sinner is able after all, so grace only assists. Both deny that the cannot is a will not.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption reasons that if man cannot believe, God cannot justly command him to believe, and the preacher need not call him. That turns moral inability into physical inability, as if the sinner were a lame man blamed for not walking. Webster saw the point in 1828: moral inability “aggravates our guilt.” The command stands, the call goes out to every hearer, and the refusal is the sinner’s own.

The second corruption runs the other way. Because the sinner is commanded, it assumes he must be able, and so makes grace a help to a will that only needs persuading. Scripture says the carnal mind is not subject to God’s law, “neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7), and that no man can come unless the Father draw him (Joh 6:44). The cure for a dead will is not encouragement but quickening (Eph 2:1).
